Contractivity of neural ODEs: an eigenvalue optimization problem

Nicola Guglielmi1 • Arturo De Marinis1 • Anton Savostianov1,2 • Francesco Tudisco3,1

1Gran Sasso Science Institute, L'Aquila, Italy {nicola.guglielmi, arturo.demarinis, anton.savostianov, francesco.tudisco}@gssi.it
2RWTH Aachen University, Germany
3School of Mathematics and Maxwell Institute for Mathematical Sciences, The University of Edinburgh, UK f.tudisco@ed.ac.uk

Abstract We propose a novel methodology to solve a key eigenvalue optimization problem which arises in the contractivity analysis of neural ODEs. When looking at contractivity properties of a one layer weight-tied neural ODE 𝑢̇(𝑡)=𝜎(𝐴𝑢(𝑡)+𝑏) (with 𝑢,𝑏∈ℝ𝑛, 𝐴 is a given 𝑛×𝑛 matrix, 𝜎:ℝ→ℝ denotes an activation function and for a vector 𝑧∈ℝ𝑛, 𝜎(𝑧)∈ℝ𝑛 has to be interpreted entry-wise), we are led to study the logarithmic norm of a set of products of type 𝐷𝐴, where 𝐷 is a diagonal matrix such that diag(𝐷)∈𝜎′(ℝ𝑛). Specifically, given a real number 𝑐 (usually 𝑐=0), the problem consists in finding the largest positive interval I⊆[0,∞) such that the logarithmic norm 𝜇(𝐷𝐴)≤𝑐 for all diagonal matrices 𝐷 with 𝐷𝑖𝑖∈I. We propose a two-level nested methodology: an inner level where, for a given I, we compute an optimizer 𝐷⋆(I) by a gradient system approach, and an outer level where we tune I so that the value 𝑐 is reached by 𝜇(𝐷⋆(I)𝐴). We extend the proposed two-level approach to the general multilayer, and possibly time-dependent, case 𝑢̇(𝑡)=𝜎(𝐴𝑘(𝑡)…𝜎(𝐴1(𝑡)𝑢(𝑡)+𝑏1(𝑡))…+𝑏𝑘(𝑡)) and we propose several numerical examples to illustrate its behaviour, including its stabilizing performance on a one-layer neural ODE applied to the classification of the MNIST handwritten digits dataset.

Keywords: Neural ODEs, Eigenvalue optimization, Contractivity in the spectral norm, Logarithmic norm, Gradient systems, ResNet

1 Introduction

Consider a ResNet [1], defined as the sequence of inner layers (for a given 𝑢0∈ℝ𝑛)

𝑢𝑘+1=𝑢𝑘+ℎ𝜎(𝐴𝑢𝑘+𝑏),𝑘=0,…,𝐾−1,

(1)

where 𝑢𝑘,𝑏∈ℝ𝑛, 𝐴∈ℝ𝑛,𝑛, ℎ is a (typically small) positive constant, and 𝜎 is a suitable absolutely continuous and strictly monotonic activation function that acts entry-wise. It is immediate to see that (1) corresponds to the forward Euler discretization of the ordinary differential equation [2], [3], [4]

𝑢̇(𝑡)=𝜎(𝐴𝑢(𝑡)+𝑏),𝑡∈[0,𝑇],

(2)

with 𝑢𝑘≈𝑢(𝑡𝑘). The robustness of (2) against adversarial attacks [5], [6], [7] is one of the key topics of investigation of modern machine learning [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13] and is tightly related to the qualitative properties of the differential equation (2), see e.g. [3], [4], [13], [14], [15], [16]. An important stability condition is that small perturbations in the input data do not lead to large differences in the output. More specifically, for any two solutions 𝑢1(𝑡) and 𝑢2(𝑡) to (2), one requires

‖𝑢1(𝑇)−𝑢2(𝑇)‖≤𝐶‖𝑢1(0)−𝑢2(0)‖,

(3)

for a moderately sized constant 𝐶. This topic has received increasing attention in recent years since it has been shown that neural ODEs can significantly benefit in terms of both robustness and accuracy by this type of forward stability [17], [18], [19]. In particular, in the context of deep learning, that is when ℎ is small, it appears clear - at least in the non-stiff case - that the stability properties of (1) and (2) are strongly related.

1.1 Contractivity

Let us consider the norm ‖⋅‖=⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/2 induced by the standard Euclidean inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩. With this choice, (3) is directly related to the notion of logarithmic norm. Let 𝑓(𝑡,𝑢)=𝜎(𝐴𝑢+𝑏) and let 𝜇∈ℝ such that

⟨𝑓(𝑡,𝑢)−𝑓(𝑡,𝑣),𝑢−𝑣⟩≤𝜇‖𝑢−𝑣‖2,

(4)

for all 𝑢,𝑣∈ℝ𝑛 and 𝑡∈[0,𝑇]. Then we have (3) with 𝐶=e𝜇𝑇. By the Lagrange theorem, we get (note that since 𝜎 is assumed to be absolutely continuous it is differentiable almost everywhere)

𝜎(𝐴𝑢+𝑏)−𝜎(𝐴𝑣+𝑏)=diag(𝜎′(𝐴𝑤+𝑏))𝐴(𝑢−𝑣),

with 𝑤=𝑠𝑢+(1−𝑠)𝑣, for a certain 𝑠∈(0,1), and it is immediate to see that the vector field 𝜎(𝐴𝑢+𝑏) - for 𝜎 absolutely continuous - satisfies (4) with 𝜇=𝜇⋆ given by

𝜇⋆=sup𝐷∈Ωsup𝑥∈ℝ𝑛,‖𝑥‖=1⟨𝐷𝐴𝑥,𝑥⟩,

(5)

where Ω indicates the set of diagonal matrices 𝐷 whose entries belong to the image 𝜎′(ℝ), i.e. 𝐷𝑖𝑖∈𝜎′(ℝ) for all 𝑖=1,…,𝑛.

Let 𝜆max(𝑋) denote the rightmost eigenvalue of 𝑋 and, for a given matrix 𝐵,

Sym(𝐵)=𝐵+𝐵⊤2.

Then, the logarithmic 2-norm of 𝐵 (see e.g. [20]) is defined as

max𝑢∈ℝ𝑛,‖𝑢‖=1⟨𝐵𝑢,𝑢⟩=𝜆max(Sym(𝐵))=:𝜇2(𝐵).

In this way we can write (5) in terms of 𝜇2 as

𝜇∗≔sup𝐷∈Ω𝜇2(𝐷𝐴).

(6)

We say that the linear map associated to 𝐵 is contractive (or strictly contractive) in 𝐿2 if 𝜇2(𝐵)≤0 (or 𝜇2(𝐵)<0, respectively), in which case we would get the stability bound (3) with 𝐶=1 (𝐶<1), i.e. for all 𝑇>0,

‖𝑢1(𝑇)−𝑢2(𝑇)‖≤(<)‖𝑢1(0)−𝑢2(0)‖,

Note that, by continuity of eigenvalues and closedness of Ω, the sup in (6) is a max. The computation of 𝜇⋆ in (6) is a non-trivial eigenvalue optimization problem, which is also considered in [4]. Its computation provides a worst-case contractivity estimate for the neural ODE (2).

Normalization

Note that for an arbitrary activation function 𝜎 we have 𝜎′(𝜉)∈[𝑚ℓ,𝑚𝑢]for𝜉∈ℝ, with 0≤𝑚ℓ<𝑚𝑢. Moreover, by the positive homogeneity of logarithmic norms we have 𝜇2(𝐷𝐴)=𝑚𝑢𝜇2(1𝑚𝑢𝐷𝐴). Thus, we can rescale the problem and consider (6) over the set Ω of diagonal matrices 𝐷 with entries in [𝑚,1], which we indicate by Ω𝑚, i.e. we let

Ω𝑚={𝐷∈𝔻𝑛,𝑛:𝑚≤𝐷𝑖𝑖≤1∀𝑖},

where 𝔻𝑛,𝑛 denotes the set of real 𝑛×𝑛 diagonal matrices.

1.2 Uniform contractivity versus asymptotic stability

As we have seen we are asking for uniform contractivity with respect to all possible trajectories, which translates into the uniform logarithmic norm property with respect to all possible diagonal matrices in Ω𝑚. Why not choose a more local approximation as in [21]? Why focus on the entire range? The reason is that this appears the only way to guarantee the stability bound (3).

Instead of asking for contractivity we may ask for a weaker asymptotic stability condition (as it is done e.g. in [3]), even if this would not guarantee a monotone reduction of the norm of the error. However this would be simple for autonomous systems but not for non-autonomous problems, as we are going to clarify.

We observe that at time 𝑡 the linearization of the neural ODE leads us to a linear problem of the form

𝑣̇(𝑡)=𝐵(𝑡)𝑣(𝑡)where𝐵(𝑡)=𝐷(𝑡)𝐴,

with a certain diagonal matrix 𝐷(𝑡)∈Ω𝑚, that is with entries in 𝜎′(ℝ). One may argue that imposing the condition that ℜ𝜆(𝑡)<0 for any eigenvalue 𝜆 of the matrix 𝐷(𝑡)𝐴 and for all 𝑡 would guarantee asymptotic stability. Unfortunately this is a necessary but not sufficient condition (see e.g. the counterexample in [22, Example 2, page 88]).

For this reason, asking that the eigenvalues of 𝐷𝐴 lie within the left complex half-plane for all 𝐷∈Ω𝑚 is not sufficient to guarantee asymptotic stability (and therefore neither contractivity, which is a stronger stability notion).

1.3 Overview of our contribution

In this paper we address several problems connected with contractivity bounds for neural ODEs. Most importantly we introduce an algorithm for the efficient computation of 𝜇∗ (see (5)) both for the constant and for the time-dependent weight matrix 𝐴=𝐴(𝑡) (see Problem (P1)). In contrast, in Problems (P2) and (P3) (which is relevant to the considered application in Section 7) the activation 𝜎 is considered fixed. In Problem (P3), in particular, the weight matrix 𝐴 is adjusted to fulfil a certain stability bound, established a priori. In more detail we deal with the following problems.

Problem (P1)

Given a matrix 𝐴, we aim to compute the smallest value 𝑚⋆ such that

𝜇2(𝐷𝐴)=0for all𝐷∈Ω𝑚⋆,

(7)

For the time-dependent case 𝐴=𝐴(𝑡), we aim to compute 𝑚⋆(𝑡) as a function of 𝑡. Relaxing the bound (7) to a moderate positive constant is also possible. This allows to identify switching functions for which the neural ODE is (uniformly) contractive. See Section 2 for the proposed two-level procedure, Section 3 for the details about the eigenvalue optimization method and Section 4 for the computation of the lower extremal slope 𝑚∗. A combinatorial relaxation, to the aim of accelerating the computation of critical diagonal matrices is proposed in Section 5.

Problem (P2)

Given a matrix 𝐴(𝑡) and a given activation function 𝜎, whose slope assumes values in [𝑚,1], we aim to approximate

𝐶=exp(∫0𝑇𝜇2(𝐷̃(𝑠)𝐴(𝑠))𝑑𝑠),

with

𝐷̃(𝑡)=argmax𝐷∈Ω𝑚𝜇2(𝐷𝐴(𝑡)),

which gives the uniform estimate ‖𝑢1(𝑇)−𝑢2(𝑇)‖≤𝐶‖𝑢1(0)−𝑢2(0)‖. Section 6 explains how to extend the methodology from the case when 𝐴 has constant coefficients. In Subsection 6.4 we also adopt a different perspective, that is fixing 𝑚 (instead of optimizing with respect to 𝑚) and still optimizing with respect to the set of diagonal matrices Ω𝑚, compute by quadrature a worst-case stability bound for the error, that is a worst case value for the constant in (3).

Moreover, in view of the application to train a real-life contractive neural ODE (used for image classification), which we will present in Section 7, we are interested in the following complementary Problem to (P1) and (P2).

Problem (P3)

Given an activation function 𝜎 whose slope assumes values in [𝑚,1] (with 𝑚 fixed a priori), and a matrix 𝐴 for which condition (7) is not fulfilled1, we aim to determine a matrix 𝐵 (which would replace 𝐴) such that

𝜇2(𝐷𝐵)=0for all𝐷∈Ω𝑚,

with ‖𝐵−𝐴‖→min with 𝐵−𝐴 belonging to a certain subset of matrices in ℝ𝑛,𝑛. This requires repeatedly solving Problem (P1), while optimizing with respect to 𝐵.

In this paper we shall restrict modifications of 𝐴 to the special form 𝐵−𝐴=−𝛿I, with 𝛿>0 as small as possible (which we will motivate in Section 7).

Extension to multilayer networks

While we focus on the single-layer case for the sake of simplicity, a variety of observations and results carry over to the multilayer setting as well, where the vector field in the neural ODE is explicitly modeled by several interconnected layers, with weight matrices 𝐴𝑖 and bias vectors 𝑏𝑖:

𝑢̇(𝑡)=𝜎(𝐴𝑘𝜎(𝐴𝑘−1…𝜎(𝐴1𝑢(𝑡)+𝑏1)…+𝑏𝑘−1)+𝑏𝑘).

We will provide details on how to extend to the multilayer case when appropriate throughout the paper (see Subsection 3.5).

1.4 Paper organization

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes in detail Problem (P1). Section 3 outlines our solution strategy, which is a two-level nested approach and is dedicated to the derivation of the inner iteration, while Section 4 is devoted to the numerical solution of the external level. In Subsection 4.5, numerical examples on small matrices, for which the solution can be derived analytically, show that the numerical solution is a very reliable approximation of the analytical solution. Section 5 deals with a combinatorial relaxation of Problem (P1), and provides important insights on its solution. We then deal with Problem (P2) in Section 6. Finally, Section 7 shows how the proposed algorithm can be employed to train a real-life contractive neural ODE (used for image classification), which is more robust and stable against adversarial attacks than the original one. The last Section 8 outlines our conclusions.

2 A two-level nested iterative method for solving (P1)

Let us consider a matrix 𝐴∈ℝ𝑛,𝑛 with negative logarithmic 2-norm 𝜇2(𝐴)<0.

Our goal is to compute

𝑚⋆=argmin𝑚∈[0,1]{𝑚:𝜇2(𝐷𝐴)=0for all 𝐷∈Ω𝑚}.

(8)

Our approach consists of two levels.

  • Inner problem: Given 𝑚>0, we aim to solve

    min𝐷∈Ω𝑚𝐹(𝐷)

    (9)

    for the functional

    𝐹(𝐷)=−𝜇2(𝐷𝐴)=−𝜆max(Sym(𝐷𝐴)),

    (10)

    with 𝐷∈Ω𝑚.

    The functional does not depend explicitely on 𝑚 but its argument 𝐷∈Ω𝑚 does. We indicate the minimum

    min𝐷∈Ω𝑚𝐹(𝐷)=−𝜆[𝑚].

  • Outer problem: We compute the smallest positive value 𝑚≤1 such that

    𝜆[𝑚]=0,

    and indicate it as 𝑚⋆.

It is obvious that 𝑚⋆ exists since Ω𝑚 is compact and non empty.

Def 2.1

We call a matrix 𝐷[𝑚]∈Ω𝑚 a global extremizer of 𝐹 if

𝐷[𝑚]=arg min𝐷∈Ω𝑚𝐹(𝐷).

Similarly, we say that 𝐷[𝑚] is a local extremizer of 𝐹 if there exists a closed neighborhood 𝜔𝑚⊂Ω𝑚 of 𝐷[𝑚] such that 𝐹(𝐷[𝑚])≤𝐹(𝐷) for all 𝐷∈𝜔𝑚.

Then we set 𝜆max(Sym(𝐷[𝑚]𝐴))=𝜆[𝑚], even in the case where the minimum is a local one.

3 Inner problem: a gradient system approach

In order to minimize 𝐹(𝐷)=−𝜇2(𝐷𝐴) with respect to 𝐷 over the set Ω𝑚, we let 𝜆 the rightmost (i.e. largest) eigenvalue of Sym(𝐷𝐴) over the set Ω𝑚. We let 𝐷(𝜏) be a smooth matrix-valued function of the independent variable 𝜏 and look for a gradient system for the rightmost eigenvalue of Sym(𝐷(𝜏)𝐴). We propose to solve this problem by integrating a differential equation with trajectories that follow the gradient descent direction associated to the functional 𝐹 and satisfy further constraints. To develop such a method, we first recall a classical result (see e.g. [23]) for the derivative of a simple eigenvalue of a differentiable matrix valued function 𝐶(𝜏) with respect to 𝜏. Here we use the notation 𝐶̇(𝜏)≔𝑑𝑑𝜏𝐶(𝜏) to denote the derivative with respect to 𝜏. Moreover, for 𝐴,𝐵∈ℝ𝑛,𝑛, we denote (with tr standing for the trace)

⟨𝐴,𝐵⟩=tr(𝐵⊤𝐴)

the Frobenius inner product on ℝ𝑛,𝑛.

Lem 3.1

[23, Section II.1.1] Consider a continuously differentiable matrix valued function 𝐶(𝜏):ℝ→ℝ𝑛,𝑛, with 𝐶(𝜏) symmetric. Let 𝜆(𝜏) be a simple eigenvalue of 𝐶(𝜏) for all 𝜏 and let 𝑥(𝜏) with ‖𝑥(𝜏)‖=1 be the associated (right and left) eigenvector. Then 𝜆(𝜏) is differentiable with

𝜆̇(𝜏)=𝑥(𝜏)⊤𝐶̇(𝜏)𝑥(𝜏)=⟨𝑥(𝜏)𝑥(𝜏)⊤,𝐶̇(𝜏)⟩.

Let us consider the symmetric part of 𝐷(𝜏)𝐴, with 𝐷(𝜏) arbitrary. Applying Lemma 3.1 to the rightmost eigenvalue 𝜆(𝜏) of Sym(𝐷(𝜏)𝐴) we obtain:

𝑑𝑑𝜏𝜆=𝜆̇=12𝑥⊤(𝐷̇𝐴+𝐴⊤𝐷̇)𝑥=12⟨𝐷̇,𝐴𝑥𝑥⊤⟩+12⟨𝐷̇,𝑥𝑥⊤𝐴⊤⟩=⟨𝐷̇,𝑧𝑥⊤+𝑥𝑧⊤2⟩=⟨𝐷̇,𝑆⟩,with𝑆=Sym(𝑧𝑥⊤),

where 𝑧=𝐴𝑥 and the dependence on 𝜏 is omitted for conciseness.

To comply with the constraint 𝐷∈𝔻𝑛,𝑛, in view of Lemma 3.1 we are thus led to the following constrained optimization problem for the admissible direction of steepest descent. In the following, for a given matrix 𝐵, diag(𝐵) denotes the diagonal matrix having diagonal entries equal to those of 𝐵.

Lem 3.2

Let 𝑆∈ℝ𝑛,𝑛 a matrix with at least a nonzero diagonal entry. A solution of the optimization problem

𝑍⋆=argmin𝑍∈𝔻𝑛,𝑛,‖𝑍‖𝐹=1⟨𝑍,𝑆⟩

(where the norm constraint ‖𝑍‖𝐹=1 is only considered to get a unique solution) is given by

𝜈𝑍⋆=−diag(𝑆)

(11)

and 𝜈 is the Frobenius norm of the matrix on the right-hand side.

Proof. The proof is obtained by simply noting that (11) represents the orthogonal projection – with respect to the Frobenius inner product – onto the set of diagonal matrices.

Observing that for 𝑆=Sym(𝑧𝑥⊤), we have diag(Sym(𝑧𝑥⊤))=diag(𝑧𝑥⊤), using Lemma 3.2, we obtain the constrained gradient for the functional (10)

𝐺=−diag(𝑧𝑥⊤).

(12)

Hence the constrained gradient system to minimize 𝐹(𝐷) is given by

𝐷̇=−𝐺=diag(𝑧𝑥⊤),

(13)

which holds until one of the entries of 𝐷(𝜏) equals 𝑚 or 1, in which case inequality constraints should be considered. Note that the ODE system (13) can be conveniently rewritten componentwise. With 𝐷=diag(𝑑1,𝑑2,…,𝑑𝑛), we get

𝑑̇𝑖=𝑥𝑖𝑧𝑖,

with (𝜆,𝑥) the rightmost eigenpair of Sym(𝐷𝐴), and 𝑧=𝐴𝑥.

3.1 Inequality constraints: admissible directions

To comply with the lower bound constraint of the diagonal matrix 𝐷(𝜏), we need to impose that 𝐷̇𝑖𝑖(𝜏)≥0 for all 𝑖 such that 𝐷𝑖𝑖(𝜏)=𝑚. For a diagonal matrix 𝐷∈Ω𝑚 we set

ℰ︀0(𝐷)≔{𝑖:𝐷𝑖𝑖=𝑚},

and we define 𝑃ℰ︀0(𝐷) as follows:

(𝑃ℰ︀0(𝐷)𝑍)𝑖𝑖={𝑍𝑖𝑖if𝐷𝑖𝑖>𝑚max(0,𝑍𝑖𝑖)if𝐷𝑖𝑖=𝑚.

Similarly, we proceed to impose the upper bound constraint: we set

ℰ︀1(𝐷)≔{𝑖:𝐷𝑖𝑖=1},

and we define 𝑃ℰ︀1(𝐷) as

(𝑃ℰ︀1(𝐷)𝑍)𝑖𝑖={𝑍𝑖𝑖if𝐷𝑖𝑖<1min(0,𝑍𝑖𝑖)if𝐷𝑖𝑖=1.

3.2 Constrained gradient system

To include constraints in the gradient system we make use of Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. Let us consider, for conciseness, only the inequality 𝐷𝑖𝑖≥𝑚 for all 𝑖. The optimization problem to determine the constrained steepest descent direction is

𝑍⋆=argmin𝑍∈𝔻𝑛,𝑛,‖𝑍‖𝐹=1,𝐷≥𝑚⟨𝑆,𝑍⟩.

(14)

Analogously to Lemma 3.2 we have that the solution of (14) satisfies the KKT conditions

𝑍=−𝐺̂,𝜈𝑖𝑍𝑖𝑖=0 for all 𝑖∈ℰ︀0(𝐷),𝜈𝑖≥0 for all 𝑖∈ℰ︀0(𝐷),

where

𝜐𝐺̂=diag(𝑆)+∑𝑖∈ℰ︀0(𝐷)𝜈𝑖𝑢𝑖𝑢𝑖⊤,

𝑢ℓ is the ℓ-th canonical versor ((𝑢ℓ)𝑖=1 if ℓ=𝑖 and (𝑢ℓ)𝑖=0 otherwise), while {𝜈𝑖} are the Lagrange multipliers associated to the non-negativity constraints, and 𝜐 is the Frobenius norm of the matrix on the right-hand side. In a completely analogous way, we can treat the inequality 𝐷𝑖𝑖≤1.

3.3 Structure of extremizers: a theoretical result

We state now an important theoretical result on the structure of extremizers (see Definition 2.1).

Thm 3.1 [necessary condition for an extremizer to assume intermediate values in (𝑚,1)]

For a given matrix 𝐴∈ℝ𝑛,𝑛 such that 𝜇2(𝐴)<0, assume that 𝐷[𝑚] is a local extremizer of the inner optimization Problem (9), and assume (generically) that the rightmost eigenvalue 𝜆 of 𝐵=Sym(𝐷[𝑚]𝐴) is simple. Let 𝑥 be the eigenvector associated to 𝜆, 𝑧=𝐴𝑥 and 𝑥𝑖 and 𝑧𝑖 are the 𝑖-th entries of the vectors 𝑥 and 𝑧, respectively.

Then the 𝑖-th diagonal entry of 𝐷[𝑚] either assumes values in {𝑚,1} (extremal ones) or - if 𝑚<𝑑𝑖𝑖<1 - the following condition has to hold true:

𝑥𝑖𝑧𝑖=0.

(15)

Proof. Assume that the 𝑖-th diagonal entry of the extremizer 𝐷=𝐷[𝑚] is equal to 𝑑, with 𝑚<𝑑<1. Now consider a small perturbation 𝛿 of such a diagonal element and consider the associated diagonal matrix

𝐷(𝛿)=𝐷+𝛿𝑢𝑖𝑢𝑖⊤∈Ω𝑚,

(with 𝑢𝑖 the 𝑖-th versor of the canonical basis of ℝ𝑛). Note that 𝐷(𝛿)∈Ω𝑚 is still admissible for |𝛿| sufficiently small.

We indicate by 𝜆=𝜆[𝑚] the rightmost eigenvalue of Sym(𝐷𝐴) and by 𝜆(𝛿) the perturbed rightmost eigenvalue of Sym(𝐷(𝛿)𝐴). By applying the first order formula for eigenvalues we obtain, for 𝜆(𝛿) the first order expansion:

𝜆(𝛿)=𝜆+12𝛿𝑥⊤(𝑢𝑖𝑢𝑖⊤𝐴+𝐴⊤𝑢𝑖𝑢𝑖⊤)𝑥+𝒪︀(𝛿2)=𝜆+𝛿𝑥𝑖𝑧𝑖+𝒪︀(𝛿2),

with 𝑥𝑖 the 𝑖-th component of the eigenvector 𝑥 and 𝑧𝑖 the 𝑖-th component of 𝑧=𝐴𝑥. If 𝑥𝑖𝑧𝑖≠0, suitably choosing the sign of 𝛿 would increase 𝜆(𝛿) for 𝛿 sufficiently small, and thus would imply 𝜇2(𝐷(𝛿)𝐴)>𝜇2(𝐷𝐴), that is a contradiction.

We are also in the position to state the following results.

Lem 3.3

Assume that 𝐷[𝑚]∈Ω𝑚 is an extremizer s.t. 𝐹(𝐷[𝑚])>0. Then min1≤𝑖≤𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑖=𝑚.

Proof. Let 𝜆=𝜆[𝑚]<0 the rightmost eigenvalue of Sym(𝐷[𝑚]𝐴). Assume that the statement is not true, that is

min1≤𝑖≤𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑖=𝑚̂>𝑚.

Then, there exists a positive 𝛾<1 such that 𝐷̂=𝛾𝐷[𝑚] has still entries in [𝑚,1], and thus belongs to Ω𝑚, i.e. it is admissible. This implies that Sym(𝐷̂𝐴) has the rightmost eigenvalue 𝜆̂=𝛾𝜆>𝜆 (which here is negative), which contradicts extremality.

Similarly we can prove the following analogous result.

Lem 3.4

Assume that 𝐷[𝑚]∈Ω𝑚 is an extremizer s.t. 𝐹(𝐷[𝑚])<0. Then max1≤𝑖≤𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑖=1.

Finally we can prove the following result.

Lem 3.5

Assume that 𝐷[𝑚]∈Ω𝑚 is an extremizer s.t. 𝐹(𝐷[𝑚])=0 and assume (generically) that 𝐷[𝑚] (as a function of 𝑚) is continuous at 𝑚. Then max1≤𝑖≤𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑖=1 and min1≤𝑖≤𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑖=𝑚.

Proof. The proof combines Lemma 3.3 and Lemma 3.4 and continuity of eigenvalues.

Rem 3.1 [Multiple eigenvalues]

Throughout the article we assume that the rightmost eigenvalue is simple. However, along a trajectory 𝐷(𝑡), a multiple eigenvalue 𝜆(𝑡) may occur at some finite 𝑡 because of a coalescence of eigenvalues. Even if some continuous trajectory runs into a coalescence, this generally does not happen after discretization of the differential equation, and so the computation will not be affected. As such situation is either non-generic or can happen generically only at isolated times 𝑡, it does not affect the computation after discretization of the differential equation.

However, close-to-multiple eigenvalues may impair the accuracy of the computed eigenpairs and should be detected numerically and treated carefully.

3.4 Numerical integration

In Algorithm 1 we provide a schematic description of the integration step. For simplicity, we make use of the Euler method, but considering other explicit methods would be similar. Classical error control is not necessary here since the goal is just that of diminishing the functional 𝐹(𝐷) (see lines 9 and 10 in Algorithm 1).

Also note that, in practice, it is not necessary to compute the Lagrange multipliers for the entries of 𝐷 that assume extremal values as in Subsection 3.2; the numerical procedure has just to check when one of the entries of the diagonal matrix 𝐷 reaches either the extreme value 𝑚 or the extreme value 1 (by an event-detection algorithm) coupled with the numerical integrator. In the first case, as in Subsection 3.1, if 𝐷𝑖𝑖=𝑚, we have to check the steepest descent direction −𝐺, and set 𝐷̇𝑖𝑖=0 if −𝐺𝑖𝑖<0 or let it unvaried otherwise. In the second case, if the entry 𝐷𝑖𝑖=1, we have to set 𝐷̇𝑖𝑖=0 if −𝐺𝑖𝑖>0 and let it unvaried otherwise.

3.5 Multilayer networks

Let us examine now networks with several interconnected layers; for simplicity we consider time-independent 𝐴𝑖 and 𝑏𝑖:

𝑢̇(𝑡)=𝜎(𝐴𝑘𝜎(𝐴𝑘−1…𝜎(𝐴1𝑢(𝑡)+𝑏1)…+𝑏𝑘−1)+𝑏𝑘).

Making use of Lagrange theorem, we get

𝜎(𝐴𝑘𝜎(𝐴𝑘−1…𝜎(𝐴1𝑢(𝑡)+𝑏1)…+𝑏𝑘−1)+𝑏𝑘)−𝜎(𝐴𝑘𝜎(𝐴𝑘−1…𝜎(𝐴1𝑣(𝑡)+𝑏1)…+𝑏𝑘−1)+𝑏𝑘)=diag(𝜎′(𝑦𝑘))𝐴𝑘diag(𝜎′(𝑦𝑘−1))𝐴𝑘−1⋯diag(𝜎′(𝑦1))𝐴1(𝑢−𝑣),

for suitable vectors 𝑦1,…,𝑦𝑘−1,𝑦𝑘. The proposed methodology extends to the study of the logarithmic norm of matrices of the form

Sym(𝐷𝑘𝐴𝑘𝐷𝑘−1𝐴𝑘−1⋯𝐷1𝐴1).

Again the functional we aim to minimize is

𝐹(𝐷1,…,𝐷𝑘)=−𝜆max(Sym(𝐷𝑘𝐴𝑘𝐷𝑘−1𝐴𝑘−1⋯𝐷1𝐴1)),

for 𝐷𝑖∈Ω𝑚 for 𝑖=1,…,𝑘. Letting

(𝐷1[𝑚],…,𝐷𝑘[𝑚])=argmin𝐷1,…,𝐷𝑘∈Ω𝑚𝐹(𝐷1,…,𝐷𝑘),

we indicate by 𝜆[𝑚] the rightmost eigenvalue of Sym(𝐷𝑘𝐴𝑘𝐷𝑘−1𝐴𝑘−1⋯𝐷1𝐴1).

Optimizing with respect to 𝑚, our task is again to find the smallest solution of the scalar equation 𝜆[𝑚]=0, which we still indicate as 𝑚⋆.

Inner iteration

In analogy to the single layer case, let us consider the symmetric part of 𝐷𝑘(𝜏)𝐴𝑘⋯𝐷1(𝜏)𝐴1, with 𝐷𝑖(𝜏) diagonal for 𝑖=1,…,𝑘. Applying Lemma 3.1 to the rightmost eigenvalue 𝜆(𝜏) of Sym(𝐷𝑘(𝜏)𝐴𝑘⋯𝐷1(𝜏)𝐴1) we obtain (omitting the dependence on 𝜏):

𝑑𝑑𝜏𝜆=𝜆̇=12𝑥⊤(Sym(𝐷𝑘̇𝐴𝑘𝐷𝑘−1𝐴𝑘−1⋯𝐷1𝐴1+𝐷𝑘𝐴𝑘𝐷̇𝑘−1𝐴𝑘−1⋯𝐷1𝐴1+⋯+𝐷𝑘𝐴𝑘𝐷𝑘−1𝐴𝑘−1⋯𝐷̇1𝐴1))𝑥=∑𝑖=1𝑘⟨𝐷̇𝑖,𝑧𝑖𝑤𝑖⊤+𝑤𝑖𝑧𝑖⊤2⟩=∑𝑖=1𝑘⟨𝐷̇𝑖,Sym(𝑧𝑖𝑤𝑖⊤)⟩,

with 𝑧1=𝐴1𝑥, …, 𝑧𝑘−1=𝐴𝑘−1⋯𝐷1𝐴1𝑥, 𝑧𝑘=𝐴𝑘𝐷𝑘−1𝐴𝑘−1⋯𝐷1𝐴1𝑥 and 𝑤1=𝐴2⊤𝐷2⋯𝐴𝑘−1⊤𝐷𝑘−1𝐴𝑘⊤𝐷𝑘𝑥, …, 𝑤𝑘−1=𝐴𝑘⊤𝐷𝑘𝑥,…,𝑤𝑘=𝑥.

This allows us to get an expression for the free gradient analogous to the single layer case.

The associated constrained gradient system is given — in analogy to (13) — by

𝐷̇𝑖=diag(𝑧𝑖𝑤𝑖⊤),𝑖=1,…,𝑘.

(16)

Every ODE in (16) is integrated with no modifications until one of the entries of 𝐷𝑖(𝜏) equals 𝑚 or 1, in which case inequality constraints should be considered.

4 Outer iteration: computing 𝑚⋆

In order to compute the smallest positive value 𝑚⋆ such that 𝜆[𝑚∗]=0 in the outer-level iteration, we have to face two issues:

  1. which initial value of 𝑚 to consider;

  2. how to tune 𝑚 until the desired approximation of 𝑚⋆.

In this section we discuss a number of results that will directly lead to a proposal for a possible way to address both these two issues. Before - in the next two subsections - we provide some insights into the problem.

4.1 The value 𝜇2(𝐴) is strongly unspecific.

Unfortunately, the only information of 𝜇2(𝐴) is very unspecific for the determination of 𝑚⋆ and the behaviour of Sym(𝐷𝐴). Here is an illuminating example, just in dimension 2. Let 𝑎11,𝑎22<0, 𝑘>0 and

𝐴=(𝑎11𝑘−𝑘𝑎22)and𝐷=diag(1,𝑚).

We have Sym(𝐴)=diag(𝑎11,𝑎22) and 𝜇2(𝐴)=max{𝑎11,𝑎22}<0; we get

Sym(𝐷𝐴)=12(2𝑎11𝑘−𝑘𝑚𝑘−𝑘𝑚2𝑎22𝑚),

having eigenvalues

𝜆1,2=12(∓𝑎112−2𝑎11𝑎22𝑚+𝑎222𝑚2+𝑚2𝑘2−2𝑚𝑘2+𝑘2+𝑎11+𝑎22𝑚),

We indicate by 𝑚⋆(𝑘) the value of 𝑚⋆ as a function of 𝑘. Choosing 𝑘=0 (𝐴 diagonal) we get 𝑚⋆(0)=0. Choosing instead 𝑘≫1, we get the first order expansion

𝜆1,2=±12(1−𝑚)𝑘+12(𝑎11+𝑎22𝑚)+𝒪︀(1𝑘).

This immediately implies that lim𝑘→∞𝑚⋆(𝑘)=1, which is consistent with Theorem 4.1, as ‖𝐴‖2=𝑘+(𝑎11−𝑎22)/2+𝒪︀(1/𝑘).

This shows that, in order to obtain a meaningful estimate of 𝑚⋆, we need more information on 𝐴 than the only logarithmic norm. For example, the non-normality of the matrix and the structure of the non-symmetric part of 𝐴.

4.2 A theoretical upper bound for 𝑚⋆

We have the following upper bound for 𝑚⋆, obtained for a general absolute norm by applying the Bauer–Fike theorem.

Recall that a general property of any logarithmic norm states that for any matrix 𝐴, it holds −‖𝐴‖≤𝜇(𝐴)≤‖𝐴‖.

Thm 4.1 [Upper bound for 𝑚⋆]

For a given matrix 𝐴∈ℝ𝑛,𝑛 such that 𝜇(𝐴)<0, assume that 𝑚⋆ solves Problem (8). Let ‖⋅‖ be an absolute norm and

𝛽(𝐴)=‖𝐴‖+‖𝐴⊤‖2.

Then, if |𝜇(𝐴)|<𝛽(𝐴),

𝑚⋆≤1−|𝜇(𝐴)|𝛽(𝐴)≔𝑚𝑢𝑏⋆<1.

(17)

If ‖⋅‖ is such that ‖𝐴‖=‖𝐴⊤‖, then |𝜇(𝐴)|<‖𝐴‖ and 𝑚⋆≤1−|𝜇(𝐴)|‖𝐴‖.

Proof. Let 𝐷=𝐷[𝑚⋆]∈Ω𝑚⋆ be an extremizer, and write 𝐷=I+𝐸. Then we have 𝜇(𝐷𝐴)=0 and

Sym(𝐷𝐴)=12(𝐷𝐴+𝐴⊤𝐷)=Sym(𝐴)+12(𝐸𝐴+𝐴⊤𝐸).

Applying Bauer-Fike theorem and exploiting the normality of Sym(𝐷𝐴), we obtain

|𝜇(𝐴)|≤‖Sym(𝐷𝐴)−Sym(𝐴)‖=12‖𝐸𝐴+𝐴⊤𝐸‖≤‖𝐴‖+‖𝐴⊤‖2‖𝐸‖=𝛽(𝐴)‖𝐸‖.

Using Lemma 3.4 and the assumption that ‖⋅‖ is an absolute norm we get that, if the largest entry of 𝐷 equals 1, ‖𝐸‖=1−𝑚⋆, otherwise ‖𝐸‖≤1−𝑚⋆. Consequently - since 𝛽(𝐴)≥|𝜇(𝐴)| - we get

|𝜇(𝐴)|≤𝛽(𝐴)(1−𝑚⋆),

which concludes the proof.

Cor 4.1

Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.1, if 𝐴 is symmetric and ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖2, then

𝑚⋆≤1−𝜅2(𝐴)−1,where𝜅2(𝐴)=|𝜆max(𝐴)𝜆min(𝐴)|

is the condition number of 𝐴 (𝜆max(𝐴)=𝜇2(𝐴) denotes the smallest eigenvalue (in modulus) of 𝐴 and 𝜆min(𝐴)=−𝜌(𝐴) the rightmost eigenvalue of 𝐴 (in modulus)).

Proof. For a symmetric matrix ‖𝐴‖2=𝜌(𝐴); moreover by the contractivity assumption, 𝜇2(𝐴)=𝜆max(𝐴) and 𝜌(𝐴)=−𝜆min(𝐴).

4.3 Iterative computation of 𝑚⋆

We aim to compute 𝑚⋆, the smallest positive solution of the one-dimensional root-finding problem

𝐹𝑚(𝐷[𝑚])=0,

(18)

where 𝐷[𝑚] denotes a minimizer of 𝐹(𝐷). This can be solved by a variety of methods, such as bisection. Theorem 4.1 suggests to start applying the outer level step with an initial value 𝑚≤𝑚𝑢𝑏⋆ (see (17)).

After computing an extremizer 𝐷[𝑚], which minimizes the functional 𝐹𝑚(𝐷) with respect to 𝐷, for fixed 𝑚, in the case when |𝐹𝑚(𝐷[𝑚])| is not below a certain tolerance, we have to further modify 𝑚, until we reach a value 𝑚̃ such that 𝐹𝑚̃(𝐷[𝑚̃])=0, which would approximate the searched value 𝑚⋆=𝑚̃. We derive now a costless variational formula and a fast outer iteration to approximate 𝑚⋆. With such formula, we aim for a locally quadratically convergent Newton-type method, which can be justified under regularity assumptions that appear to be usually satisfied. If these assumptions are not met, we can always resort to bisection. The algorithm proposed in the following in fact uses a combined Newton-bisection approach. Let 𝐷=𝐷[𝑚] be an extremizer. We denote by 𝐽=𝐽[𝑚] the diagonal matrix with binary entries (either 0 or 1), according to the following:

𝐽𝑘𝑘={1if𝐷𝑘𝑘=𝑚,0otherwise.

(19)

Next we make an assumption, which we have always encountered in our experiments.

Assumption 4.1

For 𝑚 sufficiently close to 𝑚⋆, we assume for the extremizer 𝐷[𝑚] that:

  • the eigenvalue 𝜆[𝑚]=𝜆max(Sym(𝐷[𝑚]𝐴)) is a simple eigenvalue;

  • the map 𝑚↦𝐷[𝑚] is continuously differentiable;

  • the matrix 𝐽[𝑚] is constant2.

Under this assumption, the branch of eigenvalues 𝜆[𝑚] and its corresponding eigenvectors 𝑥[𝑚] are also continuously differentiable functions of 𝑚 in a neighbourhood of 𝑚⋆. The following result gives us an explicit and easily computable expression for the derivative of 𝜙[𝑚]=𝐹(𝐷[𝑚])=−𝜆[𝑚] with respect to 𝑚 in simple terms. Its proof exploits Theorem 3.1.

Thm 4.2 [Derivative of 𝜙]

Under Assumption 4.1, the function 𝜙 is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of 𝑚 and its derivative is given as

𝜙′[𝑚]=𝑑𝜙[𝑚]𝑑𝑚=−𝑥[𝑚]⊤𝐽[𝑚]𝑧[𝑚]<0,

where 𝑥[𝑚] is the eigenvector associated to the eigenvalue 𝜆[𝑚] of Sym(𝐷[𝑚]𝐴) and 𝑧[𝑚]=𝐴𝑥[𝑚].

Proof. According to (19), we indicate by 𝐽=𝐽[𝑚] the set of indices of entries of 𝐷=𝐷[𝑚] that are equal to 𝑚. Under the given assumptions we have

𝐷𝑘′[𝑚]=1if𝐷𝑘[𝑚]=𝑚,𝐷𝑘′[𝑚]=𝛽′[𝑚]if𝐷𝑘[𝑚]=𝛽[𝑚]∈(𝑚,1),𝐷𝑘′[𝑚]=0if𝐷𝑘[𝑚]=1.

By Lemma 3.1 we have that

𝜙′[𝑚]=−𝜆′[𝑚]=−𝑥[𝑚]⊤𝐷′[𝑚]𝑧[𝑚]=−∑𝑘=1𝑛𝑥𝑘[𝑚]𝐷𝑘′[𝑚]𝑧𝑘[𝑚]=−∑𝑘∈𝐽𝐷𝑘′[𝑚]𝑥𝑘[𝑚]𝑧𝑘[𝑚].

If the index 𝑘 in the summation corresponds to a zero diagonal entry of 𝐷′[𝑚] then it does not contribute to it; similarly if 𝑘 is such that 𝐷𝑘[𝑚]=𝛽[𝑚]∈(𝑚,1), by Theorem 3.1, we have that 𝑥𝑘[𝑚]𝑧𝑘[𝑚]=0, hence the index does not contribute too. In conclusion only indices corresponding to entries equal to 𝑚 enter into the summation with value 1. This implies that

𝜙′[𝑚]=−𝑥[𝑚]⊤𝐷′[𝑚]𝑧[𝑚]=−𝑥[𝑚]⊤𝐽[𝑚]𝑧[𝑚],

which proves the statement.

In view of Theorem 4.2, applying Newton’s method to the equation 𝜙[𝑚]=0 yields the following iteration:

𝑚𝑘+1=𝑚𝑘+𝜙[𝑚𝑘]𝑥[𝑚𝑘]⊤𝐽[𝑚𝑘]𝑧[𝑚𝑘],

(20)

where the right-hand side can be computed knowing the extremizer 𝐷[𝑚𝑘] computed by the inner iteration in the 𝑘-th step. For this, we expect that with a few iterations (on average 5 in our experiments), we are able to obtain an approximation 𝑚𝑘≈𝑚⋆.

4.4 Extension to multilayer networks

The following result extends to the multilayer case an explicit and easily computable expression for the derivative of

𝜙[𝑚]=𝐹(𝐷1[𝑚],…,𝐷𝑘[𝑚])=−𝜆[𝑚]

with respect to 𝑚.

For 𝐷=𝐷𝑖, we also denote as 𝐽(𝑖)=𝐽(𝑖)[𝑚] the diagonal matrix with binary entries (either 0 or 1), according to the following:

𝐽𝑘𝑘(𝑖)={1if𝐷𝑘𝑘=𝑚,0otherwise.

Similarly to Theorem 4.2, we have the following result which gives us a formula to implement the cheap Newton-type iteration discussed in Subsection 4.3.

Thm 4.3 [Derivative of 𝜙]

Under Assumption 4.1 for all matrices 𝐷𝑖[𝑚], in a neighbourhood of 𝑚⋆, the function 𝜙 is continuously differentiable in a neighbourhood of 𝑚 and its derivative is given as

𝜙′[𝑚]=𝑑𝜙[𝑚]𝑑𝑚=−∑𝑖=1𝑘𝑤𝑖[𝑚]⊤𝐽(𝑖)[𝑚]𝑧𝑖[𝑚]<0,

where 𝑤𝑖[𝑚],𝑧𝑖[𝑚] are defined according to Subsection 3.5.

Strict contractivity

In order to impose strict contractivity one can replace equation (18) with 𝐹𝑚(𝐷[𝑚])=−𝑐, 𝑐>0. In this case, we can extend the previous results easily. In particular, the upper bound for 𝑚⋆ in Theorem 4.1 becomes

𝑚⋆≤1−|𝜇(𝐴)+𝑐|𝛽(𝐴),

and the Newton iteration step (20) takes the form

𝑚𝑘+1=𝑚𝑘+𝜙[𝑚𝑘]+𝑐𝑥[𝑚𝑘]⊤𝐽[𝑚𝑘]𝑧[𝑚𝑘].

Everything else remains exactly the same.

4.5 Illustrative numerical examples

We consider first the simple 2×2 matrix

𝐴=(−212−3),

(21)

whose logarithmic 2-norm is 𝜇2(𝐴)=𝜆max((𝐴+𝐴⊤)/2)=−0.9189… Applying Theorem 4.1 and choosing the 2-norm we get

𝑚⋆≤𝑚𝑢𝑏⋆=0.7776…

Indeed, the exact value can be computed exactly considering the extremal matrices

𝐷1=(100𝑚),𝐷2=(𝑚001),

and it turns out to be 𝑚⋆=10−46=0.202041… Applying the proposed numerical method, with a 4-digit accuracy, we get indeed the extremizer 𝐷1 with 𝑚⋆≈0.2021, which agrees very well with the exact value.

Next consider the 3×3 example,

𝐴=(−212−1−3104−3),

(22)

whose logarithmic 2-norm is 𝜇2(𝐴)=𝜆max(𝐴+𝐴⊤)/2=−0.2058…. Applying the proposed numerical method we get 𝑚⋆≈0.8023, which is obtained for the extremal diagonal matrix

𝐷=(1.00000000.80230001.0000),

where we observe that all entries assume extremal values in the interval [𝑚⋆,1].

Let us apply Newton’s method to compute 𝑚⋆, using the costless derivative formula in Theorem 4.2. The results are shown in Table 1, which shows quadratic convergence.

5 A combinatorial relaxation

The numerical integration of (9) is certainly a demanding step in terms of CPU time. However, when slightly modifying the value 𝑚 (or considering a smooth function 𝐴(𝑡)), in order to solve (9) for the new data, we propose an alternative strategy to the reintegration of (9), which is based on Theorem 3.1.

5.1 On the necessary condition (15) of Theorem 3.1

Theorem 3.1 provides an analytic condition to identify intermediate entries. Equation (15) is a codimension-1 condition. It means that for having entries of the extremizer 𝐷[𝑚] assuming intermediate values, either the 𝑖-th component of the eigenvector 𝑥 associated to the rightmost eigenvalue of Sym(𝐷[𝑚]𝐴), or the 𝑖-th component of the vector 𝑧=𝐴𝑥 have to vanish.

In the 2×2 case it is direct to prove that extremizers are either

diag(1,𝑚⋆)ordiag(𝑚⋆,1),

and cannot assume intermediate values, as one expects. We omit the proof for sake of conciseness.

In the general 𝑛-dimensional case, assume that we know an extremizer 𝐷[𝑚], whose diagonal entries only assume the extremal values 𝑚 and 1 and that the eigenvector 𝑥 of Sym(𝐷[𝑚]𝐴) and the vector 𝑧=𝐴𝑥 have entries suitably bounded away from zero. If we slightly perturb 𝑚 (or even the matrix 𝐴), then by continuity arguments we expect generically that the new extremizer has the same entry-pattern of 𝐷[𝑚], which means that the new vectors 𝑥̃ and 𝑧̃ remain close to 𝑥 and 𝑧 and thus have still non-zero entries. This remains true also for moderate changes of 𝑚. As an example, for the matrix (22) we get, using the proposed inner-outer scheme:

(𝑥,𝑥⋆)=(0.38360.35950.61580.66640.68820.6532)and(𝑧,𝑧⋆)=(1.22511.2537−1.5427−1.70550.39840.7059),

where 𝑥 indicates the rightmost eigenvector of Sym(𝐴) and 𝑧=𝐴𝑥, 𝑥⋆ the rightmost eigenvector of Sym(𝐷𝑚⋆𝐴) and 𝑧⋆=𝐴𝑥⋆. This illustrates the slight change between the above starting vectors and those in the extremizer.

The plot (as a function of 𝑚∈[𝑚⋆,1]) of the entries of 𝑥 and of 𝑧 is shown in Figure 2.

Rem 5.1

Extremizers in general are not unique. Consider for example the following matrix 𝐴 and 𝑚=0.2

𝐴=(−313/2−1−13−1−30),Sym(𝐴)=(−301/40−101/400).

Then 𝐷1=diag(𝑚,𝑚,1), 𝐷2=diag(1,1,𝑚) and 𝐷3=diag(𝑚,1,𝑚) are local extremizers, with 𝐹(𝐷1)=−1.1427, 𝐹(𝐷2)=−0.8764, 𝐹(𝐷3)=−0.8237, so that 𝐷1 is the global minimizer. Instead for the matrix 𝐴 in (22) with 𝑚=0.8 the extremizer 𝐷=diag(1,𝑚,1) turns out to be unique.

5.2 A greedy combinatorial algorithm

An algorithm to check possible extremizers only assuming extremal values is the following. Compute all possible diagonal matrices with combinatorial structure (which are 2𝑛) and compute the gradient 𝐺 for each of them. Looking at the sign of the vector 𝐺 we can assert whether a certain matrix 𝐷 is a local extremizer.

Rem 5.2 [Efficient combinatorics]

The combinatorial algorithm is very expensive when 𝑛 increases. However, starting from the knowledge of an extremizer 𝐷[𝑚], the problem of minimizing 𝐹 for 𝑚′ close to 𝑚 might be efficiently tackled by maintaining as an initial guess the extremizer 𝐷[𝑚], just replacing its entries equal to 𝑚 with the value 𝑚′, and then checking the sign of the gradient. Similarly one could tackle the problem where the matrix 𝐴 instead of 𝑚 is slightly changed, as we will see in the next section. This would allow to avoid the numerical integration of the system of ODEs to minimize 𝐹 and is somehow reminiscent of an approach based on interior point methods as opposed to simplex methods in linear programming problems.

For example (22), this gives only the detected matrix (for all 𝑚≤𝑚⋆)

𝐷[𝑚]=(1000𝑚0001).

For example, still considering Example (22), for the starting non-optimal diagonal matrix

𝐷=diag(𝑚,𝑚,1),

with 𝑚=0.9, we get 𝜆=−0.1523 and

𝐺=diag(𝟎.𝟎𝟕𝟎𝟎,−0.1602,0.0580),

which indicates that the optimality condition for the first entry is violated. Changing the value of the first entry to the opposite extremal value and modifying to

𝐷̂[𝑚]=diag(1,𝑚,1),

(23)

allows us to find the optimal solution for the problem. At this point, it is sufficient to tune 𝑚 through the scalar equation

find𝑚:𝜆max(Sym(𝐷̂[𝑚]𝐴))=0,

where 𝐷̂[𝑚] has the structure in (23) to obtain the optimal value 𝑚⋆≈0.8023.

6 Time-dependent case: problems (P1) and (P2)

We are now interested to consider the more general time-varying problem setting where 𝐴=𝐴(𝑡), for which we assume

𝜇2(𝐴(𝑡))<0.

The problem now would be that of computing the function of 𝑡

𝑚⋆(𝑡)=argmin𝑚∈[0,1]{𝑚:𝜇2(𝐷𝐴(𝑡))≤0for all matrices 𝐷∈Ω𝑚}.

(24)

We denote by 𝐷[𝑚](𝑡) an associated extremizer, that is such that 𝜇2(𝐷[𝑚](𝑡)𝐴(𝑡))=0, and by 𝑚⋆(𝑡) its smallest entry. To a given diagonal matrix 𝐷∈Ω𝑚, we associate the structured matrix

𝑆(𝐷)={𝐼1,𝐼2,𝐼3},

with

𝐼1={𝑖∈{1,…,𝑛}:𝐷𝑖𝑖=1},𝐼2={𝑖∈{1,…,𝑛}:𝐷𝑖𝑖=𝑚},𝐼3={𝑖∈{1,…,𝑛}:𝐷𝑖𝑖=𝛽𝑖∈(𝑚,1)}.

(25)

By continuity arguments, we have generically that the structure of 𝑆(𝐷[𝑚](𝑡)) is piecewise constant along [0,𝑇], that means that indexes of the entries equal to 1 and to 𝑚(𝑡), as well as those assuming intermediate values, remain so within certain intervals.

Let us consider the symmetric part of 𝐷[𝑚](𝑡)𝐴(𝑡). Applying Lemma 3.1 to the rightmost eigenvalue of Sym(𝐷[𝑚](𝑡)𝐴(𝑡)), under smoothness assumptions we obtain (where time dependence is omitted for conciseness):

0≡𝑑𝑑𝑡𝜆=𝜆̇=12𝑥⊤(𝐷̇𝐴+𝐴⊤𝐷̇+𝐷𝐴̇+𝐴̇⊤𝐷)𝑥=12𝑥⊤(𝐷̇𝐴+𝐴⊤𝐷̇)𝑥+𝛾=𝑥⊤𝐷̇𝑧+𝛾,

with 𝑧=𝐴𝑥 and

𝛾=𝑥⊤(𝐷𝐴̇+𝐴̇⊤𝐷)𝑥.

Then we have (exploiting Theorem 3.1)

∑𝑖=1𝑛𝑥𝑖𝐷̇𝑖𝑖𝑧𝑖=∑𝑖∈𝐼2𝑥𝑖𝐷̇𝑖𝑖𝑧𝑖=(∑𝑖∈𝐼2𝑥𝑖𝑧𝑖)𝑚̇⋆(𝑡).

Consequently, we obtain the following scalar ODE for 𝑚⋆(𝑡),

𝑚̇⋆(𝑡)=−𝛾(𝑡)𝜁(𝑡),𝜁(𝑡)=∑𝑖∈𝐼2𝑥𝑖(𝑡)𝑧𝑖(𝑡).

(26)

This shows that from the sign of the r.h.s. of (26) we obtain the growth/decrease of 𝑚⋆(𝑡). The resulting algorithm for the time-varying case is discussed in the next subsection.

6.1 Algorithm for the time varying problem

On a uniform time grid {𝑡𝑘}𝑘≥0 (𝑡𝑘+1=𝑡𝑘+Δ𝑡), given an extremizer 𝐷(𝑡𝑘) with minimal entry 𝑚⋆(𝑡𝑘)=𝑚𝑘⋆, we first approximate 𝑚⋆(𝑡𝑘+1) by an Euler step (where we denote as 𝐴(𝑘)=𝐴(𝑡𝑘) and 𝐴̇(𝑘)=𝐴̇(𝑡𝑘)):

𝑚𝑘+1=𝑚𝑘⋆−Δ𝑡𝛾𝑘𝜁𝑘,

with

𝛾𝑘=(𝑥(𝑘))⊤(𝐷(𝑘)𝐴̇(𝑘)+(𝐴̇(𝑘))⊤𝐷(𝑘))𝑥(𝑘),𝜁𝑘=∑𝑖∈𝐼2𝑥𝑖(𝑘)(𝑡)𝑧𝑖(𝑘)(𝑡),

with 𝑥(𝑘) eigenvector of Sym(𝐷(𝑘)𝐴(𝑘)) associated to the rightmost eigenvalue and 𝑧(𝑘)=𝐴𝑥(𝑘). Next, we update 𝐷(𝑡𝑘+1) by setting its minimal entries as 𝑚𝑘+1 and compute 𝑥(𝑘+1), i.e. the eigenvector of Sym(𝐷(𝑘+1)𝐴(𝑡𝑘+1)) associated to its rightmost eigenvalue, and set 𝑧(𝑘+1)=𝐴𝑥(𝑘+1). Then, in order to obtain a more accurate approximation of 𝑚𝑘+1⋆, we apply a single Newton step, as described in Subsection 4.3. Finally we verify that the resultant matrix 𝐷(𝑘+1)=𝐷[𝑚𝑘+1⋆] is an extremizer by checking (see (25))

𝑥𝑖(𝑘+1)𝑧𝑖(𝑘+1)>0for𝑖∈𝐼1and𝑥𝑖(𝑘+1)𝑧𝑖(𝑘+1)<0for𝑖∈𝐼2.

(27)

If, for at least one index 𝑖, one of the previous conditions (27) is violated, then an optimizer with a new structure is searched by running the whole Algorithm described in Section 3 for the matrix 𝐴=𝐴(𝑡𝑘+1).

Consider next the matrix

𝐴(𝑡)=(−2−sin(𝑡)cos(𝑡)2−2−cos(𝑡)),𝑡∈[0,𝑇],𝑇=𝜋,

(28)

which for 𝑡=0 coincides to Example (21). Figure 3a illustrates the behaviour of 𝑚⋆(𝑡).

Next, consider the matrix

𝐴(𝑡)=(−𝑡−11𝑡2+12−1𝑡−3𝑡+13−2𝑡1−2𝑡2𝑡−4),𝑡∈[0,𝑇],𝑇=1.

(29)

Figure 3b shows the sudden change of extremizer at 𝑡≈0.7. The set 𝐼2={1,2} switches to 𝐼2={3}, when 𝑡 crosses the discontinuity point for (𝑚⋆)′(𝑡).

6.3 Remarks

Applying the proposed method we obtain an accurate approximation of the extremizers 𝐷[𝑚](𝑡) for the considered problem (24) for 𝑡=𝑡𝑘,𝑘=0,1,… To have a uniform choice which guarantees contractivity we have to choose

𝑚⋆=max𝑘𝑚𝑘⋆,

which might be too restrictive. Another possibility would be that of changing the slope 𝑚=𝑚(𝑡) in the function 𝜎(𝑡). Finally, relaxing the bound

𝜆max(Sym(𝐷[𝑚](𝑡)𝐴(𝑡)))≤0to𝜆max(Sym(𝐷[𝑚](𝑡)𝐴(𝑡)))≤𝛼

for some moderate 𝛼>0, would allow maintaining control on the growth of the solution (the constant 𝐶 in (3) would be 𝐶≤e𝛼𝑇), without restricting the range of 𝜎′.

6.4 A different outlook. Problem (P2): stability bound for fixed 𝑚

Assume that 𝑚 is fixed and we want to compute a bound for the growth of the error in the solution of Problem (P2), that is to get a worst-case estimate of the type (3). We write the solution to the differential equation 𝑢̇=𝐷(𝑡)𝐴(𝑡)𝑢, 𝑢(𝑡0)=𝑢0 (with 𝐷(𝑡) unknown a priori), as

𝑢(𝑡)=Φ(𝑡,𝑡0)𝑢0.

By Grönwall Lemma, it can be shown that a bound for the norm of the state transition matrix Φ(𝑡,𝑡0) is given by

‖Φ(𝑡,𝑡0)‖≤exp(∫𝑡0𝑡𝜇2(𝐷(𝑠)𝐴(𝑠))𝑑𝑠),

for all 𝑡≥𝑡0. This means that if we compute the worst case quantity 𝜇2(𝑠)=𝜇2(𝐷(𝑠)𝐴(𝑠)) for 𝐷(𝑠)∈Ω𝑚, by applying a quadrature formula we get an upper bound for the constant 𝐶, that is

𝐶≤exp(∫0𝑇𝜇2(𝐷̃(𝑠)𝐴(𝑠))𝑑𝑠)≈exp(𝑄[𝜇2(𝐷̃(𝑠)𝐴(𝑠))])≔𝐶̃,

(30)

with 𝐷̃(𝑡)=argmax𝐷∈Ω𝑚𝜇2(𝐷𝐴(𝑡)) and 𝑄[⋅] a suitable quadrature formula, e.g. the trapezoidal rule.

Figure 4 illustrates the behaviour of

𝜇2(𝑡):=𝜇2(𝐷̃(𝑡)𝐴(𝑡))

(31)

for the matrix-valued function 𝐴(𝑡) of example (29), where for the quadrature we have used trapezoidal rule.

Rem 6.1

It is not guaranteed that there exists a trajectory 𝑢(𝑡) of the dynamical system (2) to which corresponds the critical matrix sequence 𝐷̃(𝑡). However, if such a trajectory exists, then the bound (30) is sharp.

Let us consider the Cauchy problem (2) with 𝑇=2 and the example matrix (29). Note that, for 𝑚=0.5, the problem is strictly contractive in the spectral norm. We compute the upper bound (30) for several values of 𝑚. The results are illustrated in Table 2.

7 An application: a neural network for digits classification

To conclude, we apply the theory developed in the previous sections to increase the robustness of a neural ODE image classifier. To this end, we consider MNIST handwritten digits dataset [24] perturbed via the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) adversarial attack [7].

Here, in order to maintain accuracy (the percentage of correctly classified testing images) of the neural network, the minimal slope 𝑚<1 cannot be too large. For this reason we have to face Problem (P3), since when we solve Problem (P1) with the learnt matrix 𝐴, it can happen that the value 𝑚∗ computed by solving Problem (P1) in order to get uniform contractivity of the neural ODE, might be larger than 𝑚. In this case we modify the matrix 𝐴 in order to increase the stability of the network, by simple perturbations of the form −𝛿I, that is suitably shifting 𝐴 by a scaled identity matrix. The use of optimal modifications of 𝐴 is not considered in this article, although we consider it an important research topic.

Let us recall that MNIST consists of 70000 28×28 grayscale images (60000 training images and 10000 testing images), that is vectors of length 784 after vectorization. We consider a neural network made up of the following blocks:

  1. a downsampling affine layer that reduces the dimension of the input from 784 to 64, i.e. a simple transformation of the kind 𝑦=𝐴1𝑥+𝑏1, where 𝑥∈ℝ784 is the input, 𝑦∈ℝ64 is the output, and 𝐴1∈ℝ64,784 and 𝑏1∈ℝ64 are the parameters;

  2. a neural ODE block that models the feature propagation,

    {𝑥̇(𝑡)=𝜎(𝐴𝑥(𝑡)+𝑏),𝑡∈[0,1],𝑥(0)=𝑦,

    whose initial value is the output of the previous layer, where 𝑥(𝑡):[0,1]→ℝ64 is the feature vector evolution function, 𝐴∈ℝ64,64 and 𝑏∈ℝ64 are the parameters, and 𝜎 is a custom activation function, defined as

    𝜎(𝑥)={𝑥,if 𝑥≥0,tanh𝑥,if −𝑥̄≤𝑥<0,𝛼𝑥,otherwise,

    where 𝑥̄>0 is such that tanh′(±𝑥̄)=𝛼=0.1 (see Figure 5);

  3. a final classification layer that reduces the dimension of the input from 64 to 10, followed by the softmax activation function

    𝑥out=softmax(𝐴2𝑥(1)+𝑏2),

    where 𝑥(1)∈ℝ64 is the output of the neural ODE block, 𝐴2∈ℝ10,64 and 𝑏2∈ℝ10 are the parameters, and 𝑥out is the output vector whose component 𝑖 is the probability that the input 𝑥 belongs to the class 𝑖. Recall that softmax is a vector-valued function that maps the vector 𝑥 into the vector softmax(𝑥)=𝑒𝑥‖𝑒𝑥‖1−1, where exponentiation is done entrywise.

We require the neural ODE block to be contractive, so that small perturbations added to the input, such as adversarial attacks, are not amplified.

Making use of the proposed algorithm for solving Problem (P1), we compute the smallest value 𝑚⋆ that the entries of the diagonal matrix 𝐷 can assume, such that

sup{𝜇2(𝐷𝐴),∀𝐷∈𝔻64,64 such that 𝐷𝑖𝑖∈[𝑚⋆,1]}=0,

(32)

which implies the neural ODE is contractive if 𝑚⋆≤𝛼. If the value 𝑚⋆ computed by the algorithm in Subsection 4.3 is larger than 𝛼, we set 𝛿>0 a small positive constant and replace the matrix 𝐴 by the shifted matrix

𝐴̂=𝐴−ℓ𝛿𝐼,

where ℓ is the smallest positive integer such that (32) holds for 𝐴̂ in place of 𝐴.

Note that shifting the matrix 𝐴, and thus its entire spectrum, to get 𝑚⋆ below the specified threshold 𝛼, is a greedy algorithm that allows us to obtain (32). Other strategies may be used here, including computing the nearest matrix to 𝐴 in some suitable metric while ensuring 𝑚⋆≤𝛼.

We add the proposed shifting to the standard training methodology via adjoint method [2] after parameter initialization and after each step of gradient descent to guarantee that (32) holds with 𝑚⋆≤𝛼 during training.

Rem 7.1

Observe that we apply the algorithm in Subsection 4.3 to compute 𝑚⋆ after parameter initialization and after each step of gradient descent during training, to decide if the weight matrix needs to be shifted or not. Therefore, the algorithm for solving Problem (P1) is applied each time to a different matrix.

Then, we train a first version of the above-mentioned neural network according to standard training, and we train a second version of the same neural network employing the proposed modification to the standard training. The networks are trained for 70 epochs. As a further comparison, we consider two models in the literature to improve adversarial robustness: the structural approach asymODEnet, where the vector field is constrained to be antisymmetric, i.e.

𝑥̇(𝑡)=−𝐴⊤𝜎(𝐴𝑥(𝑡)+𝑏),𝑡∈[0,1],

considered for example in [3], [15], [16], and the method SODEF by Kang et al. in [17], which is a neural ODE whose equilibrium points correspond to the classes of the considered dataset. By ensuring that the equilibrium points are Lyapunov-stable, the solution for an input with a small perturbation is guaranteed to converge to the same solution corresponding to the unperturbed initial datum.

Loss and accuracy values for all four aforementioned methods are provided in Figure 6. We eventually compare in Table 3 the test accuracy of the considered models as a function of 𝜀>0. This quantity measures the size in the 𝐿∞-norm of the FGSM perturbation applied to each testing image, i.e. if 𝑥𝑖 is a testing image, 𝑥𝑖+𝜀𝛿𝑖 is the perturbed image, with 𝛿𝑖 the FGSM attack on 𝑥𝑖 and ‖𝛿𝑖‖∞=1. Incorporating the strategy proposed here, we observe a clear improvement in robustness against the FGSM attack.

Rem 7.2

In our experiments, Table 3, the neural ODE block (b) has been numerically integrated with the forward Euler method with step size ℎ=0.05. Notice that, if the step size ℎ is sufficiently small and the neural ODE is contractive, then the discretization of the neural ODE preserves the contractivity of its continuous counterpart. Table 4 shows the performance of the model with the neural ODE block discretized using different step sizes. It is worth pointing out that the contractive behaviour seems to decrease approximately when ℎ=0.33.

8 Conclusions

In this article we have proposed a novel methodology to solve numerically a class of eigenvalue optimization problems arising when analyzing contractivity of neural ODEs. Solving such problems is essential in order to make a neural ODE stable (contractive) with respect to perturbations of initial data, and thus preventing the output of the neural ODE to be sensitive to small input perturbations, such those induced by adversarial attacks.

The proposed method consists of a two-level nested algorithm, consisting of an inner iteration for the solution of an inner eigenvalue optimization problem by a gradient system approach, and in an outer iteration tuning a parameter of the problem until a certain scalar equation is verified.

The proposed algorithm appears to be fast and its behaviour has been analyzed through several numerical examples, showing its effectiveness and reliability. A real application of a neural ODE to digits classification shows how this algorithm can be easily embedded in the contractive training of a neural ODE, making it robust and stable against adversarial attacks.
